title: A dish with a bit of miso
translation: When Hōjō Nobutoki was an old man, he told this story about Tokiyori, who ran the government in Kamakura in those days.

"One evening Tokiyori sent for me. I said I'd be right there, but I couldn't find anything proper to wear, and while I was fussing about it, a second messenger came. 'Is it that you've got nothing to wear? It's night, nobody cares what you look like. Just come.' So I went in a limp old outfit, the way I was at home.

He came out with a jug of sake and some clay cups. 'I didn't feel like drinking this on my own, so I called you. There's nothing to go with it, and everyone must be asleep by now. Go and look everywhere for something that'll do.'

So I took a light and searched every corner, and on a shelf in the kitchen I found a little clay dish with a bit of miso stuck to it. 'I found this,' I said. 'That'll do nicely,' he said, and we had cup after cup, and he was in a very good mood.
That's how things were in those days."

literal: Taira no Nobutoki, in old age, telling of old times, (said): 'Once, in the evening, I was summoned by the lay priest of Saimyōji, and while saying "At once", I had no hitatare, and as I was fussing this way and that,
a messenger came again: "Is it that you have no hitatare or such? Since it is night, even if (your dress) is odd, (come) quickly", he said, and so
I went in a limp hitatare, just as I was at home, and
he brought out a sake jug with clay cups added, (saying) "Since drinking this sake alone is dull, I sent for you.
There is no food to go with it; the people (of the house) have probably gone to sleep. Look anywhere you can for whether there is something suitable", he said, and so
I lit a paper torch and searched every corner, and on a shelf in the kitchen I found a small clay dish with a little miso stuck to it, and said, "This is what I have found", and
he said, "That will surely do", and cheerfully went on to several rounds and was in high spirits.
In that age, it was like this', he said.

notes.text: Hōjō (Ōsaragi) Nobutoki (1238–1323), of a branch of the Hōjō family, which claimed descent from the Taira; hence the 平. He later became co-signer, the second post in the Kamakura government. The 1925 edition identifies him as the son of Tomonao. {朝臣|あそん}: an old court title added after the name.

Hōjō Tokiyori (1227–1263), regent of the Kamakura shogunate and the real ruler of eastern Japan. He took Buddhist vows and lived at a temple called Saimyōji, so he is named after it. {入道|にふだう}: a layman who has taken vows. His mother is the nun of section 184.
'At once, right away'. A false friend: modern やがて means 'before long, eventually'.
{直垂|ひたたれ}: the jacket-and-trousers outfit that warriors wore when they appeared before their lord. なえたる: 'gone limp', soft from wear (the 1925 edition: the starch has gone out of the cloth).
{異様|ことやう}: 'odd, not as it should be'. The 1925 edition explains it as shabby clothing.

notes.quote: たうべむがさうざうしければ
notes.text: たうぶ: 'to eat, to drink' (the 1925 edition glosses it as たべん; modern {食|た}べる probably comes from it). さうざうし: 'dull, lonely, missing something'.
{紙燭|しそく}: a small hand light, a pine stick with an oiled tip and paper wrapped round the handle (the 1925 edition: paper coated with oil).
{献|こん}: a round of drinks. {数献|すこん}: several rounds. The most powerful man in Kamakura and his guest, drinking with a scrap of miso for a snack.

notes.quote: その世にはかくこそ侍りしか
notes.text: こそ … しか: the realis form of き, the past of things one has seen oneself. Nobutoki tells it as his own memory. The last verb, {申|まう}されき, also has き: Kenkō seems to have heard the story from Nobutoki himself.
